A **DAW** (digital audio workstation) is a tape recorder, a mixing desk and a box of instruments in one program.
BandLab, Ableton Live, Logic Pro, GarageBand, FL Studio, Reaper and Pro Tools all look different, but they are built
from the same handful of parts. These lessons teach those parts on a DAW small enough to see all at once, played by
the [Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.qmd) band's instruments. Each lesson ends with where the same thing is in
**BandLab**, **Ableton Live** and **Logic Pro**, so you can do it there next.

## Time runs left to right

Every DAW draws the song as a **timeline**: time runs left to right, one row (a **track**) per instrument. The numbers along
the top are the **ruler**, counted in **bars**. The red line is the **playhead**: where playback starts and where you are.

The counter by the buttons reads **bar . beat . sixteenth**: `3.2.1` is bar 3, beat 2, on the beat. This is how every DAW
counts, and it's why a DAW wants to know your **tempo** (BPM, beats a minute) before you start: bars only make sense at a tempo.

## Try it

1. Press **▶ Play** (or **Space**). Watch the playhead and the counter. **Space** again stops.
2. Click the ruler at bar 5: the playhead jumps there. **Enter** (or ⏮) goes back to the top.
3. Change the **Tempo** to 130 and play again. Everything is faster, nothing else changed: the notes are stored in bars and beats, not in seconds.
4. Switch on **♩ Click**, the **metronome**: a high click on beat 1, a lower one on 2, 3 and 4.
5. **Loop** (also called **cycle**): the yellow bracket under the ruler. Drag along the ruler from bar 3 to bar 4. With ⟲ Loop on,
   playback goes round those two bars until you stop it. Practising one hard spot, or writing a part over a four-bar loop,
   is most of what people use a DAW for.

<div class="mdaw" data-id="daw-timeline" data-preset="song" data-show="transport tracks"></div>

## Why bars, not seconds

A DAW that knows the tempo can put a note *on beat 3* rather than *at 4.37 seconds*. That is what lets you change the tempo
later, line notes up to the grid, copy a bar and have it fit, and hear a click in time. Audio you record is stored in seconds
but placed on the same bar grid. Set the tempo **before** you record, and record **to the click**, or the grid won't line up with
what you played.

## In other DAWs

<div class="daw-map">

| | BandLab (Studio, web/app) | Ableton Live | Logic Pro |
|---|---|---|---|
| Play / stop | Space | Space | Space |
| Back to the start | ⏮ button | Click the start of the ruler | Go to Beginning button, or click the ruler |
| Tempo | In the metronome menu | Tempo box in the Control Bar | Tempo in the control bar display |
| Counter | Time display in the transport bar | Arrangement Position in the Control Bar | Bars . beats . divisions . ticks in the control bar display |
| Metronome | Metronome button (**M**); count-in in its menu | Metronome switch (**O**); count-in in its menu | Metronome button (**K**); count-in **Shift+K** |
| Loop | Cycle button, then drag the region on the ruler | Loop switch, drag the loop brace on the ruler (Cmd/Ctrl+L loops the selection) | Cycle button (C), drag the yellow bar on the ruler |

</div>

Ableton Live has two views. The **Arrangement View** is the timeline taught here. The **Session View** (Tab switches) is a grid
of clips you launch live; leave it for later.
